analysis.one_liner: Requires app-based work platforms to disclose their pay algorithms and fees, and caps ride-hail companies' take rates at 25%.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced December 11, 2025 with 14 cosponsors (13 of 217 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans), was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that use apps to assign and manage work — like ride-hail, delivery, and other gig platforms — to tell workers in plain terms how algorithms set their pay, assign their jobs, and decide when to deactivate them. Workers would get an itemized receipt after every job and a weekly statement showing what the customer paid, what the worker received, and how much the platform kept. Ride-hail companies could keep no more than 25% of each fare (before tips), platforms could not pay different workers different amounts for the same work based on personal data, workers could not be forced into arbitration for these claims, and unions could act as workers' authorized representatives. The Labor Department and workers could enforce the rules with penalties starting in the tens of thousands of dollars per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: App-based workers — ride-hail and delivery drivers and other people whose work is assigned through an app — gain the most: they would see exactly what the customer paid and what the platform kept, learn how algorithms set their pay and trigger deactivation, be paid the same as comparable workers, and be able to sue for violations with statutory damages and protection from retaliation. Consumers gain a look at how much of their fare or fee reaches the worker. Unions and worker centers gain legal standing to receive disclosures and sue on workers' behalf. Responsible employers that do not misclassify workers also benefit from rules that keep platform competitors from cutting labor costs through opaque practices.

how_it_helps.text: Workers get written notice, in their primary language, of what data the platform collects about them, how the algorithm sets their pay and assigns work, and the specific grounds for being suspended or deactivated.

After each assignment and each week, workers receive an itemized breakdown: what the customer paid, what the worker got, the tip, miles driven, hours worked, and the take rate the platform kept — and customers receive the same breakdown for the assignment they paid for.

For ride-hail trips, the platform may keep no more than 25% of what the customer pays (excluding tips), and no worker fees that would push the effective take rate above that cap; state or local caps can go further.

Platforms cannot pay two workers different amounts for substantially similar work unless the difference reflects actual cost differences or a union contract, and cannot use individualized worker data to personalize pay.

Platforms cannot use monitoring data to infer immigration status, health, sexual orientation, religion, or union sympathy, cannot collect worker data outside time worked, and cannot sell that data; workers and their authorized representatives (including unions) can get their data within five business days.

Workers who complain or exercise rights under the bill are protected from retaliation — including deactivation — with a presumption that adverse action within 90 days of protected activity is unlawful, and workers, consumers, unions, and worker centers can sue for damages starting at $5,000 per violation.

analysis.who_pays: The covered platform companies pay: they lose the difference above a 25% ride-hail take rate, must build systems for detailed notices, itemized receipts, weekly statements, quarterly public reporting, and data retention, and face penalties of $25,000 to $100,000 per government-enforced violation plus worker lawsuits with statutory damages starting at $5,000. They also lose forced-arbitration and confidentiality agreements against their workers. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The 25% take-rate cap applies to the fare as charged, so platforms that currently keep more than a quarter of the fare would have to absorb the difference — which could lead them to raise base fares for consumers or cut bonuses and service coverage to restore margins, and the bill does not say how that cost should be shared.

The bill creates a private right of action with statutory damages starting at $5,000 per violation and reaching $20,000 or more for missed notices and reporting failures, which, multiplied across millions of workers and assignments, exposes platforms to very large litigation risk and could encourage volume lawsuits.

Section 12 limits court review of the Labor Department's implementing regulations to a three-year window filed only in the federal district court in Washington, D.C., and instructs courts to defer to the agency's interpretation — reducing the usual avenues for businesses or others to challenge how the rules are written.

The definitions sweep broadly — any platform using an automated decision system to route paid work qualifies, with the burden of proving an exclusion on the platform — so smaller and newer platforms would face the same disclosure, reporting, and penalty regime as the largest ones, with per-violation fines adjusted upward for inflation each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits for workers are real and concrete: workers currently cannot see how their pay is set or how much of the fare they generate goes to the platform, and the bill's itemized receipts, weekly statements, and take-rate cap directly target that. The honest drawbacks are on the design and cost side. A hard 25% take-rate cap may raise prices for riders or reduce service in markets where platforms operate on thin margins, and the bill does not address that tradeoff directly. The penalty structure — statutory damages starting at $5,000 and up to $20,000 or more per violation, multiplied across millions of workers and assignments — could produce large-volume litigation beyond what the disclosure harms warrant. And Section 12 narrows court review of the Labor Department's implementing rules to the D.C. district court within three years, a provision that concentrates power in the agency and would draw legitimate objection from anyone concerned about regulatory overreach. The transparency provisions are easier to defend than the pay-setting mandates and the cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and has stayed there with no hearing, markup, or floor action.

narrative.text: The Empowering App-Based Workers Act was introduced in the House on December 11, 2025 by Rep. Pramila Jayapal and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
The full action history shows no further steps after the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill — 13 of 217 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the app-based platforms it targets: with the bill sitting in committee, no federal disclosure rules or take-rate cap has taken effect, so current pay and pricing practices continue unchanged. Workers and consumers have gained nothing yet.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2025 and was joined by nine original cosponsors at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Norcross, Omar, Lee of Pennsylvania, McIver, Norton, Pocan, Takano, and Tlaib.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on December 11, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — leaving it unable to reach the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support is nearly all Democratic: 13 of the 14 cosponsors are House Democrats, with a single Republican cosponsor out of 223 House Republicans.

industries.note: The bill caps what they keep per trip at 25% of the fare and requires per-trip and per-week disclosure of prices, pay, and take rates; several companies currently keep well above that share by their workers' own reports. Their interest in keeping the current split runs directly against the drivers and riders the bill protects.

industries.industry: On-demand delivery and other gig platforms
industries.note: They face the full disclosure regime, a ban on individualized algorithmic pay, data-handling limits, penalties of $25,000 to $100,000 per violation, and enforceability stripped from their arbitration and confidentiality agreements. Their savings from opaque pay-setting come at workers' expense.

Vendors that collect or interpret platform-worker data face four-year record retention, a ban on selling or transferring the data, and joint liability with the platform for violations. Their interest tracks the platforms they serve rather than the workers whose data they handle.

They gain standing to receive workers' disclosures as authorized agents and to sue on workers' behalf, giving them a foothold in organizing app-based workforces that are otherwise hard to reach. Their role here runs alongside workers' interests.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills at this stage — introduced with a small cosponsor list and referred to committee — never get a hearing or a vote, and this one has shown no committee movement. With only 14 supporters out of 435 House members, majority-party control of the Education and Workforce Committee, and no Senate companion action, the realistic path is that it stalls in committee for the remainder of the 119th Congress unless it attracts substantially broader support.
